title: Dual-Nitrate-Releasing Electrospun PAN Nanofiber Separators to Suppress Post-Cycle Corrosion Through Anti-Corrosive Interphase Engineering in Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Seochan Hong, Nayeon Kim, Jae Hyeong Park, Gwan Hyeon Park, Hayoung Lee, Jiyoung Lee et al.
abstract: Lithium (Li) metal suffers from continuous chemical corrosion in liquid electrolytes, critically limiting the calendar life of lithium metal batteries (LMBs). Conventional anti-corrosion strategies have primarily focused on stabilizing the initial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), while corrosion after prolonged cycling remains insufficiently understood. Here, we demonstrate for the first time that repeated Li plating/stripping accelerates subsequent Li corrosion during rest by amplifying the electrolyte-accessible surface area and destabilizing the interphase. We define this cycling-history-dependent degradation as post-cycle corrosion, a critical pathway limiting long-term LMB performance. To address this challenge, we design an electrospun AgNO 3 /Bi(NO 3 ) 3 -embedded polyacrylonitrile (PAN) nanofiber separator (ABPN) as a sustained reservoir of anti-corrosive interphase precursors, implementing the first sustained-release strategy based on dual nitrate species. The continuously supplied nitrate species form a low-solubility, inorganic-rich SEI composed of Li 3 N, LiN x O y , and LiF, suppressing parasitic Li–electrolyte reactions. Concurrently, the in situ formed Li–Ag/Li 3 Bi dual-alloy interphase combines complementary alloy functions to enable uniform Li deposition, enhance interfacial structural stability, and suppress cycling-induced surface-area amplification, thereby mitigating post-cycle corrosion. Consequently, ABPN-based full cells deliver 159 mAh g −1 at 5 C and retain 73.9% capacity after 500 cycles with a 4 h rest after each charge, whereas polypropylene ( PP)-based cells retain only 55.5% after 200 cycles. This work establishes post-cycle corrosion as a critical degradation mode and advances anti-corrosion design beyond SEI stabilization toward simultaneous regulation of interphase chemistry and cycling-induced morphological evolution.

title: Super‐Toughness Self‐Healing Composite Solid Electrolyte With Structured Interfacial Reconstruction Enabling Fast Ion Transport and Stable Interface for High‐Performance Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Feng Zou, Zhihong Yao, Bo Peng, Shixin Liu, Runwei Mo
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium–metal batteries are widely regarded as a key direction for next‐generation energy storage systems due to high energy density. However, LiNi 0 . 8 Co 0 . 1 Mn 0 . 1 O 2 ||Li battery systems face severe challenges in practical application, including lithium dendrite growth, interfacial side reactions and structural degradation of high‐nickel cathodes. Here, we proposed a versatile modification strategy combining in‐situ interfacial transformation with polymer phase regulation to fabricate self‐healing solid polymer electrolyte with fast ion transport and stable interface. This strategy not only constructs fast ion channels and suppresses hydrofluoric acid production by in‐situ converting Li 2 CO 3 on the Li 6.4 La 3 Zr 1.4 Ta 0.6 O 12 surface into Li 2 PO 3 F interfacial layer, but also induces the transition of PVDF from α‐phase to high polarity β‐phase using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid to promote lithium salt dissolution and reduce Li + migration resistance. The as‐prepared electrolyte exhibits extended electrochemical voltage windows (5.13 V), high room‐temperature ionic conductivity (1.694 mS cm − 1 ), excellent thermal stability (200°C), high elongation at break (422.6%), and superior cycling stability (89.4% retention after 500 cycles at 1 C). A non‐destructive monitoring method based on d p /|d Q | and d T /|d Q | differential signals has been developed to track electrochemical‐mechanical‐thermal responses during battery operation. This work provides an effective strategy for designing solid polymer electrolytes with high ionic conductivity and interfacial stability.

title: Anchored Fluoro‐Shielded Solvation for Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Kaihua Wen, Tengsheng Chi, Junyao You, Lei Mao, Xinxin Zhu, Yan‐Bing He et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)‐based polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for solid‐state lithium metal batteries owing to their favorable overall electrochemical properties. However, conventional PVDF‐based polymer electrolytes suffer from uneven solvation distribution, discontinuous ion‐transport pathways, and unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces caused by residual solvents and porous PVDF frameworks. Herein, we report an anchored fluoro‐shielded solvation strategy to construct a high‐performance PVDF‐based polymer electrolyte. By integrating polyanionic anchoring sites with fluorinated shielding segments, the optimized electrolyte enables spatially distributed anion‐rich solvation pathways, homogeneous Li + transport, and robust LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). The polymer electrolyte delivers a high ionic conductivity of 1.26×10 −3 S cm −1 , a Li + transference number of 0.69, an oxidative onset potential of 5.27 V, and a critical current density of 6.4 mA cm −2 . Spectroscopic and interfacial analyses reveal that the anchored fluoro‐shielded solvation structure promotes LiF‐rich SEI formation and suppresses solvent decomposition. Consequently, Li||LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 batteries retain 80.2% capacity after 2000 cycles under high‐voltage and high‐rate conditions of 4.5 V and 5 C. This work highlights anchored fluoro‐shielded solvation as an effective molecular design principle for advanced polymer electrolytes toward practical high‐voltage and high‐rate solid‐state Li metal batteries.

title: N‐Heterocyclic Molecular Additives Enable Solvation and Interfacial Chemistry Regulation for High‐Stability, High‐Rate, and High‐Capacity Lithium Metal Anodes
authors: Fujie Liu, Linglin Xia, Tingting Zhao, Juying Zhou, Jianfang Lu, Cong Liu
abstract: ABSTRACT Most electrolyte additives enable long‐term Li plating/stripping at <3 mA cm − 2 , non‐applicable to practical Li‐metal batteries (LMBs) operating at ≥5 mA cm − 2 and ≥ 5 mAh cm − 2 . Here, we report an interaction chemistry that enables simultaneous solvation and interfacial regulation by exploring a novel N‐heterocyclic molecule (i.e., TPTC)—comprising an N‐heterocyclic core and four pyridine units–as an efficient additive for achieving ultra‐stable Li‐metal anodes under practical conditions. Electron‐rich N atoms in TPTC serve as ion‐dipole interaction sites, inducing competitive coordination that weakens Li + solvation and enhances Li + migration in the bulk electrolyte, which homogenizes Li + concentration near the interface, favoring high‐rate Li deposition. TPTC also adsorbs on Li surface to construct a protective layer with a low interfacial de‐solvation barrier, which–together with low‐barrier Li + transport through heterocyclic cavities–facilitates uniform Li deposition. Meanwhile, electron‐deficient C–H sites in pyridine weakly interact with TFSI − , forming an anion‐rich interfacial region that in situ decomposes into an inorganic‐rich interphase, affording high‐flux Li + transport. This synergy allows stable Li plating/stripping at 10 mA cm −2 /10 mAh cm −2 for 3000 h. Paired with a high‐loading LiFePO 4 cathode (∼15 mg cm −2 ) and thin Li (∼100 µm), the cell maintains 87.8% capacity after 400 cycles.

title: Zwitterionic Thermoplastic Polyurethane‐Based Quasi‐Solid Polymer Electrolytes for Lithium Metal Batteries With Machine‐Learning‐Assisted Mechanistic Insights
authors: Hongbin Na, Kyeonghyeon Nam, Yonghyuk Lee, Sung‐Kon Kim
abstract: ABSTRACT This study presents a quasi‐solid‐state electrolyte based on zwitterionic thermoplastic polyurethane (QS‐Z‐TPU) for lithium metal batteries. Unlike conventional quasi‐solid polymer electrolytes that mainly serve as passive liquid‐electrolyte reservoirs, QS‐Z‐TPU is designed as an active ion‐regulating matrix via phosphorylcholine‐derived zwitterionic groups in the TPU framework. The resulting electrolyte combines the elasticity and film‐forming capability of TPU with dual‐site ion regulation, where phosphate sites coordinate Li + while quaternary ammonium and urethane N‐H groups immobilize TFSI − anions. This design enhances electrolyte affinity while suppressing destructive swelling due to ionic crosslinking. QS‐Z‐TPU exhibits high ionic conductivity, a wide electrochemical stability window, and an enhanced Li + transference number. Machine‐learning‐assisted molecular modeling further reveals that the zwitterionic oligomer stabilizes separated LiTFSI configurations through cooperative Li + coordination and TFSI − association, substantially reducing the energetic penalty for ion‐pair separation. This regulated ion environment promotes uniform Li + flux at the lithium metal interface and facilitates the formation of a stable inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase. Consequently, QS‐Z‐TPU enables stable Li plating/stripping and improves the cycling stability and rate capability of LFP|Li full cells, further validated in flexible pouch‐cell demonstrations. These findings highlight zwitterionic molecular engineering as an effective strategy for interface‐stabilizing quasi‐solid electrolytes.

title: Fundamental Design Principles and Engineering Strategies of Liquid‐Phase Electrolytes for Highly Durable Rechargeable Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Yaoda Wang, Zhong Jin
abstract: Lithium (Li) metal has emerged as the premier anode candidate in next-generation high-energy-density batteries due to its ultrahigh theoretical capacity and ultralow electrochemical potential. However, critical technical barriers persist in Li metal anode implementation, such as uncontrolled Li dendrite growth and persistent interfacial side reactions. Acting as the mediating agent between cathodes and anodes, electrolytes critically determine battery overall performance. Taking solvent-salt-additive components as the entry point, adopting liquid-phase electrolyte engineering strategies to optimize electrolyte composition and regulate solvation structure can not only address the inherent issues of Li metal anodes, but also endow Li metal batteries with desired performances, including high safety, high-voltage tolerance, fast-charging capability, and wide-temperature operation. In this review, the design principles of reliable liquid-phase electrolytes for Li metal batteries are discussed in detail. The essential liquid-phase electrolyte engineering strategies, including designing new-type salt/solvent molecular architectures, restructuring salt-solvent combination systems, incorporating electrolyte additives with various functions, utilizing (localized) high-concentration electrolytes, and developing brand-new electrolyte formulations for adapting to different temperature ranges, are comprehensively summarized. Moreover, emerging design strategies, future design considerations, and remaining challenges in electrolyte engineering are highlighted, with the aim of pointing out potential opportunities to propel the practical development of Li metal batteries.

title: Ionic‐Ligand‐Assisted Transport in Fluorinated Poly(ionic liquid) Electrolytes Enables 515 Wh Kg −1 Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Zhicheng Wang, Kun Liang, Chenlu Wang, Ju Ren, Wei Li, Haifeng Tu et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Decoupling ionic conductivity from polymer segmental relaxation while maintaining interfacial stability remains a pivotal challenge for solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs). In this study, we construct an ionic‐ligand‐assisted transport framework by copolymerizing a fluorinated acrylate polymer with a poly(ionic liquid) (PIL) and optimizing the lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) salt concentration. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that cationic PIL moieties strongly anchor FSI − anions, creating anion‐rich, spatially correlated coordination pathways that facilitate efficient Li + hopping. The optimized electrolyte exhibits a high ionic conductivity (0.38 mS cm −1 ) and an exceptional Li + transference number (0.77) at 30°C. The fluorinated backbone and PIL synergistically expand the oxidative stability window to 4.94 V and promote an inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the Li‐metal anode. Consequently, Li||Cu cells cycle stably for over 400 cycles with 99.1% average Coulombic efficiency. Solid‐state Li||LiNi 0.9 Co 0.05 Mn 0.05 O 2 (NCM90) cells retain ≈81.0% capacity after 600 cycles at 4.3 V, and ≈83.1% capacity after 200 cycles at 4.5 V. Moreover, a high‐energy‐density (515 Wh kg −1 ) solid‐state pouch cell with an ultrathin Li anode (50 µm) and a high‐loading NCM90 cathode (≈56 mg cm −2 ) delivers stable cycling and exceptional safety. This ionic‐ligand regulation paradigm provides critical mechanistic insights for designing high‐performance and high‐safety solid‐state batteries.

title: Operando Mapping of Population Phase Separation and Lithium‐Plating Dynamics in Graphite Electrode Using Optical Microscopy and Microstructure Modeling
authors: Heng Huang, Yang Li, Xuekun Lu, Xinyu Liu, Yang Li, Huanyue Zhang et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT The fast‐charging capability of phase‐separating graphite electrodes is largely constrained by heterogeneous reaction kinetics and sluggish mass transport at both the particle and electrode scales, which increase the risk of parasitic lithium plating and associated safety concerns. A deeper mechanistic understanding of the interplay among phase‐separation dynamics, electrode microstructure, and lithium‐plating propensity is therefore essential for guiding the rational design of advanced electrode architectures and fast‐charging protocols. Here, we combine operando optical microscopy with three‐dimensional microstructure‐resolved phase‐field modeling to resolve the interplay between phase separation and lithium plating. Microscopy captures stages evolution, phase mode transitions and structural dynamics across the particle population and at the single‐particle level, which is driven by the slow interfacial reactions. Non‐equilibrium phase‐field simulations elucidate the kinetic control mechanisms governing phase transitions as the current varies. Importantly, a new mechanism of lithium plating associated with interfacial ohmic resistance is identified. Based on these insights, we evaluate particle‐size‐distribution design and use thermal activation as a mechanistic probe to resolve how temperature alters phase‐separation pathways and lithium‐plating behavior. These results may serve as a foundation for improving the physical understanding and driving optimization of fast charging protocols for lithium‐ion batteries.

title: Beyond Isolated Active Sites: Adjacent Single‐Atom‐Nanoparticle Electronic Coupling Enables Lateral Lithium Growth
authors: Jun Zhang, Yu Dong, Zhenyu Wang, Tongxiang Chen, Xudong Sun, Jing Li et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Precise host regulation remains pivotal for dendrite‐free lithium metal anodes (LMAs). While maximizing isolated single‐atom sites improves initial Li nucleation, their uniform adsorption energetics inherently confine Li to these initial sites, favoring localized vertical accumulation over lateral growth. Here we propose an adjacent single‐atom‐nanoparticle electronic coupling strategy to break this thermodynamic bottleneck. Via coordination‐mediated laser direct writing, we construct a hierarchical porous graphene host comprising ultrafine Co nanoparticles and adjacent Co single atoms. Precursor preorganization and the ultrafast, non‐equilibrium kinetics of laser processing concurrently drive in situ graphitization and Co‐species reconstruction, effectively suppressing the aggregation in conventional thermal synthesis. Mechanistically, rather than relying on isolated thermodynamic traps, interfacial electronic coupling reconstructs the local d ‐band center and establishes a directed spatial Li adsorption‐energy gradient. This thermodynamic driving force compels Li to sequentially occupy neighboring sites, effectively precluding localized vertical accumulation. Owing to this spatially regulated deposition, the high‐loading Li||LiFePO 4 full cells retain 71.4% capacity after 1000 cycles at 2 C. This adjacent electronic coupling strategy transcends the isolated active sites paradigm, opening a new dimension for interfacial electronic‐structure regulation in practical LMAs.

title: Bifunctional Additive Enabled Thermoresponsive Electrolytes With Dual‐Mode Manipulation Toward Safe Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Xue Yang, Xiao Hang Guo, Ming Hui Zhang, Yu Hao Huang, Yong Li, Bao Ning Zhu et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Thermal safety issues arising from electrolyte instability at elevated temperatures pose a critical challenge for lithium (Li) metal batteries (LMBs). Thermoresponsive electrolytes offer a promising solution, yet battery systems with high‐rate capability and reliable thermal protection have not been realized. Herein, we introduce a bifunctional LiNO 3 additive into a high‐volume‐fraction vinylene carbonate‐based thermoresponsive electrolyte (HVCE‐N) to enhance the performance of LMBs at room and elevated temperatures. Notably, the introduction of the LiNO 3 additive modifies the solvation structure of Li + and forms a Li 3 N/LiN x O y solid electrolyte interface with high ionic conductivity. Under thermal shock, HVCE‐N undergoes a rapid liquid‐to‐solid phase transition upon free radical polymerization to form a polymer network. More importantly, LiNO 3 can regulate the free radical concentration to control the degree of polymerization, thereby preserving high ion transport capability even after phase transition. As a result, a Li||NCM811 cell based on HVCE‐N exhibits high‐rate performance from 1C to 10C, and stable cycling at 100°C. When subjected to a thermal shock of 200°C, HVCE‐N suppresses thermal runaway for Li||NCM811 pouch cell. This electrolyte design offers a new strategy to develop highly safe LMBs with high‐rate performance.

title: Redirecting Bond Cleavage in Sacrificial Prelithiation via Dual‐Side Separator Engineering for Anode‐Free Lithium Batteries
authors: Junyu Zhang, Xiangrui Tian, Jiawen Tang, Yunsong Li, Wenzhuo Tan, Peiwen Fan et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Anode‐free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs) promise extreme gravimetric and volumetric energy densities but suffer from irreversible active lithium loss, sluggish desolvation kinetics, and dendritic proliferation. Herein, we report a catalyst‐induced bond‐cleavage redirection concept to unlock efficient sacrificial prelithiation, implemented via a dual‐side functionalized separator. On the cathode side, a 5 µm MoC 1‐x /NC‐0.3Co coating redirects Li 2 C 2 O 4 decomposition from high‐barrier Li–O cleavage to preferential C─C bond scission. Theoretical calculations and operando characterizations confirm this mechanistic shift, lowering the delithiation potential to 3.79 V at 60°C with a 99.5% Li + utilization rate. To safeguard the liberated lithium inventory against depletion, the anode side integrates a PSSLi‐PFPE bilayer. This coating accelerates Li + desolvation and drives the in‐situ construction of a LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase, enabling Li symmetric cells cycling for over 1700 h (1.0 mAh cm −2 , DOD = 80.7%). Bridging fundamental bond kinetics with practical engineering, the assembled 1.0 Ah anode‐free pouch cell (NCM811||MoC 1‐x /NC‐0.3Co‐LCO/PE/PSSLi‐PFPE||Cu) achieves gravimetric and volumetric energy densities of 458.6 Wh kg −1 and 1005.2 Wh L −1 , a power output of 989.1 W kg −1 , retaining 80.1% capacity after 100 cycles. This non‐invasive separator strategy provides a unified framework connecting bond kinetics to practical cell manufacturing, charting a feasible avenue for high‐energy AFLMBs.

title: Mineral Particle Suspensions in Carbonate Electrolyte Enable LiF‐Rich Interphases for Durable Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Hongmei Liang, Lisha Mou, Jin Leng, Aiping Wang, Li Wang, Yongsheng Han et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT The solid electrolyte interphase in lithium metal batteries determines cycling stability but often suffers from the incomplete decomposition of fluorinated components. Herein, we demonstrate that suspending LiF and Li 2 O particles in a carbonate‐based electrolyte promotes the defluorination of fluoroethylene carbonate and lithium hexafluorophosphate. These particles preferentially adsorb fluorinated electrolyte species and induce electronic polarization, thereby modulating their redox reactivity and facilitating interfacial decomposition toward LiF. The generated LiF, together with the trace dissolution and interfacial reprecipitation of suspended LiF particles, continuously enriches the electrode surface with LiF‐rich inorganic species. This process results in the formation of a bilayer interphase on both the lithium metal anode and LiNi 0.6 Co 0.2 Mn 0.2 O 2 cathode, featuring a flexible inner layer and a dense LiF‐rich outer layer. The resulting interphase suppresses lithium dendrites, mitigates parasitic reactions, and enables 2400 h of stable cycling in symmetric cells and 85.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles in full cells. By introducing suspended LiF/Li 2 O particles to regulate the interfacial decomposition of fluorinated electrolyte species, this work provides an effective electrolyte‐design strategy for constructing robust interphases in lithium metal batteries.

title: A Tailored Multifunctional Lithium Organosilicate Salt Constructing Robust Interphases for High Voltage Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Ningxiang Zhu, Gaojie J. Xu, Guansheng Chen, Shenghang Zhang, Zhilin Yang, Yu Zhao et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have attracted extensive attention due to their high energy density. However, when lithium (Li) metal is paired with high‐voltage cathode materials, its practical application is limited by issues such as continuous oxidative decomposition of electrolytes and the incompatibility between electrolytes and aggressive electrodes. Herein, we synthesize a fluorinated lithium organosilicate salt (i.e., lithium fluorobis(fluoropinacolatoborato)silicate, LiPBS) to address the aforementioned challenges. The results show that the LiPBS can form a protective and rigid‐flexible cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) on the cathode surface. Simultaneously, PBS − readily forms a coordination ion pair (CIP) with Li + , constructing an inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the Li anode. Furthermore, Si─O groups in the LiPBS can effectively scavenge HF and H 2 O from the electrolyte. These advantageous properties enable LiCoO 2 (LCO, 1.89 mAh cm −2 )/Li (50 µm) coin and pouch cells to exhibit excellent cycling performance at high voltages and elevated rates‒for example, retaining 82% capacity after 250 cycles at 1 C and 4.5 V, compared to 80% retention after only 67 cycles for the LiPF 6 ‐based counterpart. This performance is maintained even at an elevated temperature of 50°C. This work highlights the crucial role of lithium organosilicate salt in determining the electrochemical performance of LMBs.

title: Durable Interphase Incorporating Cross‐Linked Polymer Enables Long‐Calendar‐Life Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Jia‐lin Li, Jianxin Tian, Qiang Zhang, Yan‐Bin Gao, Dong‐Hao Zhan, Qiankui Zhang et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT The practical deployment of lithium (Li) metal batteries is hindered by not only cycle life but also calendar life. The poor calendar life stems from both the repeated reconstruction of the solid‐electrolyte interphase (SEI) during cycles and, particularly, the continuous growth of SEI during storage. Herein, a durable SEI with high mechanical stability against volume fluctuations and superior passivation capability to suppress electrolyte permeation is demonstrated by integrating inorganics and a cross‐linked polymer into the SEI. Concretely, a cross‐linked polymer with high modulus and low swelling is in‐situ incorporated among the inorganics of an anion‐derived SEI. The elastic modulus of the SEI is significantly increased from 1.63 to 4.37 GPa, and the compactness of the SEI is also improved to suppress electrolyte permeation. Consequently, the cycle life and calendar life of Li metal coin cells are extended by 73% (from 190 to 329 cycles) and 129% (from 1553 to 3561 h), respectively. Furthermore, a prototype pouch cell (506 Wh kg −1 ) undergoes 124 cycles. This work establishes an effective strategy that concurrently improves the mechanical and passivation performance of the SEI, tackling the critical challenge of calendar life in Li metal batteries.

title: Mass‐Charge Regulatory Microdomains Enable Coupled Structural and Interfacial Stabilization of Durable 3D Lithium Metal Anodes
authors: Jiajie Pan, Jieying Hua, Yusi Wang, Haoan Yuan, Junhao Li, Kaixiang Shi et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Three‐dimensional (3D) architectures can stabilize lithium (Li) metal anodes (LMAs) by mitigating localized charge accumulation and volume fluctuation, but the enlarged anode/electrolyte interfaces aggravate parasitic reactions and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) evolution. In this study, we constructed a mass‐charge regulatory microdomain‐functionalized LMA (MCRM‐Li) by mechanically integrating a hierarchically structured NiS x framework with Li foil to address this structure‐interface dilemma. The embedded conductive matrix partitions bulk Li into ordered microdomains and establishes an interconnected electron transport network to dissipate localized current density. Simultaneously, the in situ formed Li 2 S‐rich interphase suppresses solvent attack and induces Li 2 S/LiF‐enriched SEI formation during cycling, thereby homogenizing Li + flux and facilitating interfacial Li + diffusion. Consequently, the symmetric cell based on MCRM‐Li delivers an ultralong lifespan of over 5380 h with dendrite‐free Li deposition. Moreover, LiFePO 4 full cells retain 94.1% capacity after 1000 cycles at 2 C. This work provides a coupled structural‐interfacial design paradigm for durable lithium metal batteries through regional control of electric‐field distribution and interfacial mass transfer in operating 3D LMAs.

title: “Lithium‐Free” Anode Solid‐State Batteries Enabled by 3D Structured Miec Garnet
authors: G. V. Alexander, Aoife Zuercher, Jay Yvonne Easter, Christopher Tang, William Schubert, Jack E. Gritton et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Inhomogeneous lithium nucleation at the current collector‐solid electrolyte interface leads to unstable lithium growth and poor reversibility in “lithium‐free” solid‐state batteries. Here we show that stable lithium formation occurs within a mixed ionic and electronic conducting (MIEC) garnet scaffold. The intrinsic electronic conductivity of the porous framework enables lithium to nucleate uniformly along internal pore surfaces, rapidly forming a conformal lithium coating, thus establishing electronic connectivity at very low lithium volume fraction. This uniform lithium formation dramatically lowers anode impedance, enabling reversible lithium plating and stripping with Coulombic efficiencies of a previously unheard‐of 99.95%. When paired with NMC811 cathodes, bilayer (MIEC(P)‐LLZ(D)) “lithium‐free” full cells exhibit stable, highly reversible cycling at practical current densities, all at room temperature with no applied pressure. The interplay between lithium volume fraction and impedance is quantitatively modeled, transforming the understanding of lithium nucleation in a “lithium‐free” cell from an empirical interface problem to a percolation‐governed transport process, guiding the design of electronically percolating scaffolds for next‐generation solid‐state batteries.

title: A Safety‐Engineered Organic–Inorganic Composite Separator Enabling Fire‐Extinguishing and Dendrite‐Free Lithium Metal Battery Operation
authors: Yichuan Dai, Mingyan Chuai, Xinyu Deng, Zigeng Wu, Yongjie Feng, Dingyi Zhou et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT The limited thermal stability, mechanical fragility, and flammability of polyolefin separators impose inherent constraints on the safety and lifespan of lithium metal batteries. Although surface‐coating strategies have been widely explored, single‐component coatings, for example, Al 2 O 3 or polyimide, are unable to simultaneously address dendrite suppression, anti‐thermal shrinkage, and flame retardant. Given these critical challenges, we report a design strategy of multifunctional organic‐inorganic composite separator: (a) an ammonium polyphosphate and poly(acrylic acid) cross‐linked polymer provides intrinsic fire‐retardant behavior and features an electrolyte‐philic characteristic that facilitates Li‐ion transport; (b) a rigid Al 2 O 3 network embedded in the polymer matrix resists thermal shrinkage and blocks dendrite penetration through synergistic SEI protection layers rich in Li 3 N and Li 3 PO 4 . Together, these synergistic functions enable Li||Li cells to cycle stably for 2000 h and deliver long‐term stability in LFP||Li full cells (88% capacity retention over 1000 cycles). Moreover, the average heat release rate per unit area (0.04°C min −1 cm −2 ) of this battery during thermal runaway is markedly suppressed compared to those (0.3°C min −1 cm −2 ) of batteries using polyolefin separators, pouch cells incorporating this separator consistently exhibit rapid self‐extinguishing behavior during repeated ignition tests. This integrated safety‐centric architecture offers a practical pathway towards intrinsically safe, long‐life lithium metal batteries.

title: Copper‐Governed Divergence of Lithium Deposition Modes in Anode‐Free Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Sida Huo, Li Wang, Yue Wang, Yihui Bai, Meng Li, Ming Fang et al.
abstract: ABSTRACT Anode‐free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs) maximize energy density by eliminating anode host materials, but their lifetime is governed by Li deposition on the current collector (CC)—a heterogeneous nucleation and growth process. Current research mainly focuses on electrolyte or artificial interphase engineering, whereas how the CC's physical structure dictates initial deposition behavior remains unclear. Here, we show that the microstructure of Cu foils induces two distinct Li deposition modes: localized nucleation‐selective growth (LS) and distributed nucleation‐competitive coalescence (DCC). Using HLCu and nmCu as model interfaces, we elucidate the evolution pathways of these modes. By integrating AFM, iSCAT, ToF‐SIMS and operando EIS‐DRT, we reveal mode‐specific differences in nucleation sites, interfacial kinetics, and the coupling between morphology, mechanical response, and side reactions. The LS mode generates loose, non‐uniform Li deposits with strong gas evolution, whereas the DCC mode enables dense, continuous, and kinetically stable Li layers. This work demonstrates that the CC is not a passive substrate but a critical component that determines the deposition mode and performance degradation. Optimizing the physical structure of the CC interface offers a key strategy—beyond electrolyte and interphase design—for long‐life AFLMBs.

title: Lewis Acid‐Enabled Functional SEI/CEI Design for Durable Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Luning Miao, Li Ma, Fuchen Song, Gang Huang, Xinbo Zhang
abstract: ABSTRACT The development of practical lithium metal batteries requires facile strategies that simultaneously stabilize anode and cathode interfaces while eliminating their native surface oxides. However, the reported research could rarely achieve this dual functionality. Herein, we have developed a dual‐side‐modification strategy using tributylphosphonium tetrafluoroborate (TBPFB) as a Lewis acid to synchronously eliminate the heterogeneous native oxide layers and reconstruct multifunctional inorganic interfaces on both the cathode and anode. The constructed artificial interface on the lithium anode contains LiF, LiBO 2 , Li 3 P, and Li 3 PO 4 , boosting the anode stability by reducing the Li + desolvation barrier and enabling uniform Li + transport. Meanwhile, the LiF‐rich LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) cathode interface suppresses side reactions and particle cracking, protecting the cathode from transition metal dissolution. Based on the benefits brought by the multifunctional interfaces, the Li||Li symmetric cells achieve a cycling lifespan of over 1700 h, while the Li||NCM811 full cells retain 77% capacity after 500 cycles. Additionally, a 2 Ah pouch cell with an energy density of 423.1 Wh kg −1 maintains over 90% capacity after 100 cycles. This work provides a simple but highly efficient surface modification strategy that stabilizes the most critical interfaces in lithium metal batteries.

title: Screen-Printed Li Arrays with Reinforced Interphase as Ultrathin Anodes for High-Energy–Density Liquid- and Solid-State Batteries
authors: Wenting Liu, Zhenyao Wei, De Ning, Zhenhuan Lu, Fengping Zhang, Xuhao Wang et al.
abstract: Abstract High-energy–density lithium metal batteries, either liquid or solid state, require ultrathin Li anodes, but their implementation is hindered by poor Li processability in fabrication and inhomogeneous Li plating behaviours upon cycling. This work addresses these challenges through a mask-patterned discrete array using a molten salt-derived Li nanocomposite. The screen-printing strategy circumvents the poor wettability of molten Li on copper that causes high Li|Cu contact angle and non-uniform Li spreading, thus fabricating ultrathin Li foils with equivalent thicknesses below 30 μm. Concurrently, the molten salt-derived inorganic nanoparticles in Li favour homogeneous Li deposition and induce inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase to jointly suppress active Li consumption. The resulting Li array (10–28 μm) anodes demonstrate remarkable performance in both liquid- and solid-state systems, achieving high energy densities up to 504 Wh kg −1 /1071 Wh L −1 and stable cycling over 260 cycles with high-loading cathodes. This integrated approach resolves both fabrication and cycling challenges of ultrathin Li anodes and offers an alternative solution for high-performance liquid-/solid-state batteries.

title: A Pyridine Mediator Enables High‐Efficiency, Long‐Cycling Anode‐Less/Free Lithium–Sulfur Batteries With Li 2 S Cathodes
authors: Sijia Huang, Pengfei Sang, 孙昊婧, Yongzhu Fu, Xiang Li
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium sulfide (Li 2 S) is a promising high‐capacity cathode material. Importantly, it can provide lithium source, enabling lithium batteries with an anode‐less/free configuration. However, Li 2 S suffers from poor conductivity, high polarization, low material utilization, as well as the shuttle effect, severely restricting the long cycling performance of batteries. Herein, lithium pyridine‐2‐thiolate (PySLi) is proposed as a multifunctional mediator for Li 2 S‐based anode‐less/free batteries. It is revealed that PySLi can modify the reaction pathway of Li 2 S, comprehensively enhancing its electrochemical redox kinetics and stability. Results show that the energy efficiency of the Li||Li 2 S cell with PySLi stabilizes at ∼80% in the full‐scale range from 0.1 C to 3 C rate, which is much higher than that without PySLi (49% at 0.1 C and 22% at 3 C). The stability of the lithium metal anode is also improved, maintaining a high coulombic efficiency of >98% for 200 cycles and stable lithium stripping/plating behavior for 1000 h. Moreover, an anode‐free battery based on Li 2 S cathode works normally for 150 cycles, and an anode‐less pouch cell retains steady performance for 200 cycles. This multifunctional mediator provides a new strategy for the application of Li 2 S and stable anode‐less/free batteries with high energy density.
